title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation

paper.title: ObsSpec : Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
paper.abstract: Abstract Tool-using agents alternate between model generation and tool execution, waiting for each tool call to complete before starting the next generation. This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec , an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec .

This sequential execution is costly during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), which requires large batches of multi-turn rollouts. We introduce ObsSpec , an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that uses a small world model to predict tool outputs while the environment executes, allowing the policy to begin its next generation early. ObsSpec retains speculative work only when the predicted and actual observations match exactly, making rollout collection lossless, while co-training keeps the world model up to date as the policy learns. On terminal-use tasks, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster. Using these predictions, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies. Across controlled experiments, we characterize the regimes in which ObsSpec reduces agent latency under shared policy resources. Finally, because ObsSpec overlaps policy generation with tool execution, it is architecturally compatible with existing techniques for accelerating RL. Code is available at https://github.com/kylemontgomery1/verl-recipe/tree/obsspec/obsspec . 1 Introduction Tool-using agents solve complex tasks by alternating between model generation and tool execution ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) . A terminal agent, for example, generates a shell command, waits for a sandbox to execute it, observes the output, and then generates its next command. In our experiments with terminal agents, tool execution makes up nearly half of the agent’s latency. The cost is significant during agentic reinforcement learning (RL), where each policy update requires hundreds or even thousands of concurrent, multi-turn rollouts. Observation speculation predicts a tool’s output while the tool executes, allowing the policy to begin generating its next action before the actual observation arrives. Recent works apply this technique at inference time, substantially reducing agent latency ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Saberi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Applying observation speculation to RL introduces three requirements. First, rollout collection must be lossless: rollouts contain no mispredicted observations or actions generated from them. Second, speculation should accelerate rollout collection under shared policy resources. Because many rollouts run concurrently, speculative policy generations can slow other rollouts by competing for the same policy resources. Third, predictions must remain accurate as the policy learns. Policy updates can change the rollout distribution, so a frozen world model may become less accurate as training progresses. Figure 1: Across policy sizes, ObsSpec reduces latency and increases asynchronous rollout throughput with similar rewards. We introduce ObsSpec , an observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL designed around these requirements. A small world model predicts the next observation while the environment executes the corresponding action, allowing the policy to begin its next generation as soon as the prediction completes, without waiting for tool execution to finish. When the actual observation arrives, we retain the speculative generation only if the predicted and actual observations match exactly and discard it otherwise. This keeps rollout collection lossless. To limit contention with non-speculative policy generations, we bound how far ahead the pipeline speculates (depth) and how many alternative observations it predicts (breadth). We evaluate how these limits affect rollout latency under shared policy resources. Finally, we co-train the world model with the policy, using actual observations as supervision to keep its predictions accurate as training proceeds. Experiments on terminal-use tasks show that ObsSpec predicts tool outputs quickly and accurately. For example, predictions from a 0.6B world model exactly match actual observations in 66.4% of attempts and arrive roughly 16 times faster than tool execution. ObsSpec reduces agent latency by 9.3% and 14.2% for 8B and 32B policies, respectively, and increases asynchronous rollout throughput by up to 11.5%. By overlapping policy generation with tool execution, ObsSpec is architecturally compatible with other RL acceleration techniques, including fully asynchronous rollout scheduling ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Piché et al., 2025 ) , sample-efficient RL algorithms ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025a ; Shrivastava et al., 2026 ) , low-precision inference ( Xiao et al., 2023 ; Qiu et al., 2026 ) , speculative decoding ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Pham et al., 2026 ) , and multi-token prediction ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In short, we make three contributions. • We introduce ObsSpec , a lossless observation speculation pipeline for agentic RL that co-trains a lightweight world model with the policy. • We show that tool outputs can often be predicted accurately and substantially faster than the corresponding tool calls can be executed. ObsSpec translates this opportunity into up to 14.2% lower agent latency and 11.5% higher asynchronous rollout throughput on terminal-use tasks. • We show how world model size, speculation depth, and speculation breadth affect rollout latency under shared policy resources, and how co-training helps maintain prediction accuracy as the policy learns. 2 Approach 2.1 Problem Setup To solve a task x x , a tool-using agent takes a sequence of actions toward the task’s goal. Each action is a tool call, and its output is an observation. By overlapping policy generation with tool execution, ObsSpec reduces agent latency by up to 14.2%. 2.2 Speculating Tool Outputs Tool outputs are often highly predictable. In a terminal setting, for example, many commands such as changing directories return no output, while others repeat information already available in the history, such as the contents of a previously viewed file. If an observation can be predicted before the corresponding tool call finishes executing, the policy could begin generating its next action without waiting for the tool output. Recent works exploit this opportunity during inference through observation speculation: they predict tool outputs and start the next policy generation before the tool call finishes executing ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Saberi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . We study how to adapt this inference-time technique to an RL setting. Applying observation speculation to RL introduces three requirements. First, lossless rollout collection requires that a rollout contain no mispredicted observations or actions generated from them. Existing inference-time methods for observation speculation may accept semantically similar observations ( Saberi et al., 2026 ) or reuse speculative tool execution when the next action matches ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , which can violate this requirement and corrupt training. Second, speculation should accelerate rollout collection under shared policy resources. Existing methods assume request latencies are independent, and evaluate proprietary models such as GPT-5, where large deployments absorb speculative generations without noticeably slowing other requests ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , or estimate latency savings through simulation or trajectory replay ( Saberi et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . In contrast, RL systems generate many rollouts concurrently to make full use of the allocated policy resources ( Sheng et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Piché et al., 2025 ) . Consequently, speculative requests compete with non-speculative requests for the same resources, so the gains from speculation must offset the slowdown in policy generation. Third, predictions must remain accurate as the policy learns. Policy updates can change the tool calls the agent makes, the states it visits, and the observations it receives. A world model fit to an earlier distribution may consequently become less accurate, making speculation less effective. To address these challenges, we propose ObsSpec , an observation speculation pipeline shown in Figure 2 . After the policy samples a t a_{t} , the pipeline starts executing it in the environment and simultaneously asks a small world model q ϕ q_{\phi} to predict the resulting observation o ^ t ∼ q ϕ ( ⋅ ∣ h t , a t ) \widehat{o}_{t}\sim q_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{t},a_{t}) .
